series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/4] block: do not issue background swap bios as root
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to modify the behavior of bio_issue_as_root_blkg() to not issue background swap bios as root, allowing cgroup IO controllers to throttle such I/O. The change is motivated by the fact that some swap writes are best effort and can be throttled without stalling indefinitely on swap writes.

review_comments.author: Christoph Hellwig
review_comments.summary: Questioned whether REQ_BACKGROUND implies that I/O can be throttled, suggesting that the caller should tolerate a failure if it is foreground paging.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Sep 28, 2026 at 10:18:36AM +0200, Alexandre Ghiti wrote:
> bio_issue_as_root_blkg() issues every REQ_SWAP bio as root, bypassing
> the cgroup IO controllers, because reclaim cannot stall indefinitely on
> swap writes. Some swap writes are not urgent though: zswap writeback is
> best effort.
> 
> Such a bio cannot simply drop REQ_SWAP: dm-crypt and dm-thin rely on it
> for limit_swap_bios, which caps in-flight swap bios to avoid a memory
> deadlock, see commit a666e5c05e7c ("dm: fix deadlock when swapping to
> encrypted device").

Is that true?  REQ_BACKGROUND very much implies the I/O can the throttled
and thus better not be foreground paging, and thus the caller should be
able to tolerate a failure.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/4] mm/zswap: turn shrink_memcg_cb()'s argument into a flags word
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the `shrink_memcg_cb()` function in the zswap module to accept a flags word instead of a boolean pointer as an argument. The flags word allows callers to pass additional information, specifically whether the walk stopped at an entry already in the swap cache. This change does not introduce any functional changes but rather provides a more flexible way for callers to interact with the function. The patch defines a new flag `ZSWAP_SHRINK_SWAPCACHE` and updates the function's logic accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/4] mm/zswap: allow writeback to be throttled by the cgroup IO controllers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the cgroup IO controllers to throttle zswap writeback operations by introducing a new 'throttled' flag in the swap_io_ctx structure. When this flag is set, the write operation is issued as background I/O instead of being exempt from cgroup throttling, which avoids priority inversion and ensures that memory reclaim is not stalled for other workloads.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/4] mm/zswap: move reclaim-driven writeback to a kworker
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the reclaim-driven writeback of zswap to a kworker, improving performance by avoiding stalls in application threads or kswapd. The kworker writes back swap entries in batches of SWAP_CLUSTER_MAX while holding a reference on the memcg, and reports nothing freed until the worker runs. This change is necessary because cgroup IO controllers throttle zswap writeback, causing stalls that were observed in production workloads.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This RFC patch series aims to improve the performance of zswap by making its shrinker writeback work with iocost. The current implementation causes a large production workload to be slower when zswap is enabled, due to two main issues: (1) zswap writeback being charged as debt and causing stalls in application allocations, and (2) throttled writes sleeping in their submitter, which can be an application thread. The patches propose to throttle zswap writeback instead of making it REQ_SWAP, and move the reclaim-driven writeback to a per-lruvec kworker.

version_history.subject: [PATCH 2/2] btrfs: commit after deleting an unused block group if system space is low

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where deleting multiple unused block groups in one transaction can fail due to insufficient system space, resulting in an -ENOSPC error. To solve this issue, the patch introduces a mechanism that checks for low system space and commits a single transaction to delete a single block group at a time. This approach allows the system to recover unallocated space and improves the chances of successfully allocating system chunks. The patch modifies the btrfs_delete_unused_bgs function in fs/btrfs/block-group.c to implement this new behavior.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

version_history.subject: [PATCH 1/2] btrfs: allocate additional SYSTEM space earlier

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance issue in Btrfs file systems where large block devices can accumulate thousands of system chunks, leading to slow deletion of unused block groups when the file system is filled up and then freed en-masse. The problem arises because the current implementation allocates new system chunks only when the space left is smaller than the reservation for a single chunk tree update. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function `system_space_needed` that estimates the upper bound on bytes needed to modify every leaf in the chunk tree and allocates additional system space earlier, ensuring that all block groups can be deleted in one transaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm/huge_memory: make thp_underused() work for mTHP folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the thp_underused() function to make it work with mTHP folios, which are larger than PMD-sized folios. The function is made size-aware instead of hardcoded to PMD-sized folios. A new helper function, thp_can_be_underused(), is introduced to check if a folio can be underused based on the number of zero-filled pages and the sysctl maximum value. This change will allow anonymous mTHP folios to be added to the deferred split list in future patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios that can never be underused
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios in the Linux kernel by skipping the queuing of folios that can never be underused, reducing unnecessary work and improving performance. The default khugepaged/max_ptes_none setting causes the shrinker to never split these folios for being underused, so they are not queued. This change is particularly important for a subsequent patch that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, as it prevents small mTHP orders from taking the list_lru lock on every anonymous fault.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm/memory: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP (huge page) folios to the deferred split list in the Linux kernel's memory management code. This allows for underused splitting of huge pages, which can help reclaim unused parts of large memory allocations when the system is under memory pressure. The patch addresses a problem where fully mapped huge pages that are mostly zero-filled do not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The solution involves mirroring the behavior for PMD-sized folios and adding a check to minimize overhead on common fault paths.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by enabling 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base pages. The patches split underused anonymous mTHP folios, which are not currently reclaimed under memory pressure. Patch 1 makes the thp_underused() function size-aware to accommodate larger folio sizes. Patch 2 optimizes existing behavior by keeping folios that can never be found underused off the deferred split queue. Patch 3 queues anonymous mTHP folios from map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what is already done for PMD folios. The patches aim to provide a solution for deploying 2M THP=always on arm64 without causing memory regressions.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Lance Yang noted that the use of an absolute value for khugepaged_max_ptes_none as both the mTHP underused threshold and the PMD collapse threshold is inconsistent, leading to different values being used depending on whether it's applied in mTHP or PMD context. He suggested using a per-order value instead, which would also allow preserving the current behavior by leaving max_ptes_none unset.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 16, 2026 at 03:44:34PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
>PMD-sized THPs that are mostly zero-filled are reclaimed under memory
>pressure by the deferred split shrinker, but this is not done for mTHP
>folios. At Meta we would like to deploy 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k
>base pages, as 2M provides the contpte benefits while the PMD size there
>(512M) is too big to use. However, 2M THP=always causes memory regressions
>unless the unused portions of those folios can be broken down and
>reclaimed.
>
>v1 did two things. It scaled khugepaged_max_ptes_none down per folio order and
>it queued every anonymous mTHP folio. David objected to the scaling since
>collapse had already rejected proportional scaling as either letting the memory
>footprint creep or being confusing to reason about. David and Barry separately
>objected to the queuing, which adds list_lru lock contention on every anonymous
>fault, and hurts lower-order use cases such as Android's order-2-only
>configuration. Johannes suggested keeping khugepaged_max_ptes_none absolute and
>simply not queuing folios that could never exceed it, which addresses both.
>
>Read as an absolute count, khugepaged_max_ptes_none also implies the
>smallest folio that takes part in underused splitting. A 2M folio on 64k
>base pages is 32 pages, so the knob has to be set below 32 for those to
>be queued at all, and any folio with no more pages than the value stays off
>the queue entirely.

Em ... I'm not sure max_ptes_none should also become the mTHP underused
threshold ...

Say we're on arm64 with 64K pages and set it to 16. Khugepaged PMD
collapse uses 16, while mTHP collapse turns the same value into 0. With
this series, an order-5 (2 MiB) mTHP enters the deferred split queue
because it has 32 pages, and is considered underused once more than 16
pages are zero-filled. So the same knob means 16, 0, and 16 depending on
where it is used ... That's a bit odd ... no?

Would a per-order value make more sense here?

An unset value could preserve the current behavior, while an explicit
value could control both mTHP collapse and underused splitting. That
would also give us a way to leave max_ptes_none as the legacy fallback
instead of adding more meaning to it :)

Cheers, Lance

>Patch 1 makes thp_underused() folio-size aware. Today it only ever sees
>PMD-sized folios, so it assumes HPAGE_PMD_NR pages throughout. Patch 3

>when the region is almost fully populated. That is fine for the deployment

>

Author: Nico Pache <nico.pache@linux.dev>
Date:   Fri Jun 5 10:14:11 2026 -0600

    mm/khugepaged: generalize __collapse_huge_page_* for mTHP support

    generalize the order of the __collapse_huge_page_* and collapse_max_*
    functions to support future mTHP collapse.

    The current mechanism for determining collapse with the
    khugepaged_max_ptes_none value is not designed with mTHP in mind.  This
    raises a key design issue: if we support user defined max_pte_none values
    (even those scaled by order), a collapse of a lower order can introduces
    an feedback loop, or "creep", when max_ptes_none is set to a value greater
    than HPAGE_PMD_NR / 2.  [1]

    With this configuration, a successful collapse to order N will populate
    enough pages to satisfy the collapse condition on order N+1 on the next
    scan.  This leads to unnecessary work and memory churn.

    collapse support to two max_ptes_none values, 0 and HPAGE_PMD_NR - 1.

      available mTHP order.

    any non-supported max_ptes_none value is configured with mTHP enabled.

    khugepaged_max_ptes_swap parameters, and will fail if it encounters a

all contend on one lruvec, running 80 threads x 16 MB x 200 loops.

running perf lock contention on folio_lruvec_lock_irqsave ("lock wait"
is all 80 threads summed):

    size                 contentions   lock wait   folios/MB

    mTHP-16K          4203612      392.8 s        64
    mTHP-32K          2064073      190.5 s        32
    mTHP-64K           212012        1.7 s          16
    mTHP-128K          117993        1.8 s           8
    mTHP-256K           64532        4.2 s           4
    mTHP-512K           32485        3.1 s           2
    mTHP-1024K           4313        0.3 s           1
    mTHP-2048K            725        0.1 s           0.5

mTHP-16k results in more lock contentions (though I didn't see a
runtime regression. I saw that 16k comes out a bit faster than 4k in
wall time), but 64k results in significantly less. For mTHP-32k, I see
less time overall spent waiting, but 2x the lock contention.

I re-ran the benchmark with the 3 patches in this series applied, with
the khugepaged/max_ptes_none sysfs value set to 0 so every folio gets
queued (the worst case) and measured the queueing cost by switching
shrink_underused on/off. I saw:

      size                 runtime delta between on/off   folios/MB
      mTHP-16K             +15.8%                                64
      mTHP-32K             +11.5%                                32
      mTHP-64K              +1.1%                                16
      mTHP-128K             +1.2%                                 8
      mTHP-256K             -0.6%                                  4
      mTHP-512K             +0.5%                                 2
      mTHP-1024K            -1.2%                                 1
      mTHP-2048K            -0.3%                              0.5

which mirrors the same pattern/trend as above (eg regresses at the 16k
and 32k cases, but not for 64k+).

I ran a perf analysis and the delta doesn't come from the deferred
split list's own lock, but actually from folio_lruvec_lock_irqsave:

      shrink_underused             0            1
      runtime                     6.00s           6.86s           +14.3%
      lruvec contentions     4206376      4234324      +0.7%
      lruvec wait            406.4 s           485.8 s         +19.5%
      avg wait                96.5us           114.5us
      list_lru_lock           absent            absent

The lruvec contentions count doesn't move much (0.7%) but the time
spent waiting goes up 19.5%. I think that's coming from the free path
rather than the fault path. In folios_put_refs(),
__page_cache_release() keeps the lruvec locked across the whole batch,
and from what I'm seeing, folio_unqueue_deferred_split() gets called
from inside that loop. I don't think your lru cache series helps this
directly since it batches on the add side but this cost is coming from
the free side inside a section that's already batched, but I think it
should help indirectly, since there would be less lruvec pressure /
contention overall. I'm not 100% sure about this, but think it might
be possible to move the unqueue from the deferred list to outside the
lruvec lock hold, though I need to look more into this.

For now though, I think it makes sense to have a hard-coded minimum
folio size for the underused shrinker, as you and David suggested.
Based on the results above, I think having 64k as the cut-off makes
sense.

Agreed. And if/when collapse gains proportional support later on,
having split already scaled means one value governing both instead of
two.

Agreed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in the Linux kernel's memory control module to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing implementation in memcg. The new struct page_counter_stock_pcp preserves the functionality of its memcg counterpart and adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended, but rather a copy of existing code from memcg.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be stock-aware, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving the same semantics as try_charge_memcg's greedy charge attempt and refill behavior. The function now takes two new parameters: may_batch, which preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios, and nr_charged, which reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge. This change is intended to improve memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high without affecting existing functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more flexibility in managing memory usage. The transition is done while preserving the legacy user-visible memory <= memory+swap invariant. The patch also removes unused memcg code and prepares for future work on introducing additional page counters without affecting cgroup v2 users.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 RESEND 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock (bank) to the memsw page counter in Linux's memory control system, allowing it to operate independently of the main memory bank. The patch introduces new functions for scheduling and draining the stock, ensuring that failed allocations do not replenish the newly attached memsw stock. It also preserves user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant by reporting memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes as the larger raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch moves the stock abstraction from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is intended to improve performance and scalability for future work on multiple page_counters in a single memcg. The existing seven-slot per-CPU design and drain policy are retained. For memcg v1 users, this decouples the memory and memsw stocks, potentially leading to different sizes of precharged cache for each. To maintain an invariant between these two stocks, the patch reports the larger value of usage_in_bytes for memsw reporting.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which is already holding a valid mm_users reference. The redundant mmgrab() call is dropped to simplify the code and avoid potential issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/13] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, rather than relying on the caller to increment a shared counter. The daemon can now keep its own counter without needing to test who called the collapse function. This change simplifies the code and improves maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/13] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the bitmap 'mthp_present_ptes' in the mm/khugepaged module to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed various checks. This change does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to improve clarity of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/13] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and implementation of the collapse feature from the khugepaged.c file. The collapse feature is used for page migration and memory compaction. The new header file defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control parameters, as well as two constants related to page table entries. This separation improves code organization and maintainability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/13] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct called collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller before asking for a collapse. The policy includes limits on missing, swapped-out or shared PTEs in a window, as well as other settings such as whether to look at used ranges and how to handle MADV_FREE'd pages. The patch replaces scattered tests throughout the collapse path with reads from the collapse_policy struct, simplifying the code and removing the need for khugepaged to look up who called it. The policy is filled once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/13] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the kernel handles memory collapsing by allowing it to work out the allowed orders for a VMA only once per VMA, rather than once per PTE table. This is done by passing the mask of allowed orders from collapse_possible_orders() directly to the functions that need it, and sampling it once per VMA instead of once per table. review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the collapse engine and its callers being intertwined, proposing to separate them by introducing an interface and splitting the call in two with the lock as the boundary.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

[ This is the first of the cleanups I said I would front-load ]

There is no line between the collapse engine and the callers that ask for
a collapse.  khugepaged.c holds both, and they reach into each other.

 - Sixteen tests through the collapse path read cc->is_khugepaged to work
   out what they are allowed to do, when every one of those decisions was
   made by the caller before it asked.

 - collapse_single_pmd() does both halves of a collapse behind one call and
   drops mmap_lock somewhere in the middle.  Which of its paths dropped it
   is not something a caller can see, so it hands back a bool and the
   caller keeps track.

 - MADV_COLLAPSE's implementation -- the walk over the user's range, the
   per-PMD loop, the errno translation -- sits in khugepaged.c, which is
   the daemon's file.

So: draw the line.  State what a caller allows in a policy, split the call
in two with the lock as the boundary, and move the syscall to madvise.c.
What the engine offers is then three calls, with the lock state written
down against each, and a policy the caller fills for itself:

    collapse_control_init(cc)         once, before the first table
    collapse_policy_*(&cc->policy)    what this caller allows
    collapse_scan_pmd(vma, addr, ...) per table, under mmap_lock
    collapse_run_pmd(mm, addr, ...)   when a scan found work, no mmap_lock

The engine stays in khugepaged.c for now; what changes is that it has an
interface, and that neither half has to ask about the other.  madvise.c
gains the operation it should have had all along.

Changes since v3
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260916093145.4022188-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 5: the PTE limits come as two sets, struct collapse_limits for a
   PMD-sized window and one for anything smaller, and the strict_sub_pmd
   flag goes.  The warning for a max_ptes_none between 0 and the maximum
   moves to where khugepaged fills its policy.  The fields only one side
   reads are prefixed anon_ or file_.  collapse_policy_forced() is
   collapse_policy_madvise() (David).

 - Patch 8 is new: collapse_file() is called from collapse_single_pmd()
   rather than from inside collapse_scan_file(), so the file scan stops at
   the decision before the scan/run split.  The writeback retry and the
   tracepoint change move into it, so patch 9 is only the split (David).

 - Patch 9: no collapse_control_release().  It had nothing to release in
   this series; it comes back with the engine, where init allocates.  The
   check that the last scan was run stays at the top of collapse_scan_pmd()
   (David).

 - Patch 10: the changelog says why the lock boundary belongs to the
   caller (David).

 - Patch 11: both callers pass their TVA type as the literal it is rather
   than reading it back from the policy (David).

 - Patch 12: kerneldoc on every function collapse.h declares (David).

 - Acked-by from David Hildenbrand on 1-4, 6 and 7; Reviewed-by from
   Baolin Wang on 10.  Reviewed-by dropped from 5 and 9, which changed.

Changes since v2
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260910120238.2529819-1-kirill@shutemov.name/

 - Patch 8: the file scan returns SCAN_PTE_MAPPED_HUGEPAGE as it is and
   the run is handed what the scan returned, so it goes straight to
   retracting the PTE table when it sees it.  The scan_retract_only flag
   and the result round trip go, and the two copies of the file put become
   one helper (Zi).  Patches 9-12 follow the new signature.

 - Patch 8: mthp_collapse() and collapse_huge_page() read the orders and
   the referenced and swapped-out counts from collapse_control instead of
   taking them as arguments (Baolin).

 - Patch 11: each interface function is documented where it is defined,
   with the lock state on entry and exit.  The overview in collapse.h
   stays (Zi).

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan on 8 and 9, and from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang
   on 5 and 10.

Changes since v1
================

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/cover.1788533997.git.kas@kernel.org/

 - Rebased onto mm-new with Vernon Yang's tracepoint fixes in it.  Patch 8
   no longer merges the two calls to each scan tracepoint, since the base
   already has one; its changelog now says what the status field reports.

 - Patch 3: nr_occupied_ptes is nr_eligible_ptes, and the mthp_collapse()
   comment counts eligible PTEs too (Zi, Baolin).

 - Patch 4: no comments on the two constants (Baolin).

 - Patch 5: one line per policy field (Baolin).

 - Patch 8: the file side is split like the anonymous one (Zi).
   collapse_scan_file() runs under mmap_lock in the scan and only reads;
   collapse_file() runs in the run.  See Behaviour below.

 - Reviewed-by from Zi Yan and Baolin Wang on 1-4, 6 and 7.

Patches
=======

The first three stand alone and can be taken separately:

  1  drop the mmgrab() MADV_COLLAPSE has held since 7d8faaf15545
  2  count collapses in khugepaged's own walk, where the daemon's
     bookkeeping belongs
  3  rename cc->mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes, which is what a set
     bit means

Then the interface, in order:

  4  add collapse.h, and move enum scan_result, struct collapse_control
     and the two constants into it
  5  struct collapse_policy, filled by the caller; the is_khugepaged
     tests become field reads, and the flag goes
  6  drop collapse_possible(), a wrapper that only turns a mask into a bool
  7  collapse_control_init_scan() is a per-table reset, so name it
     collapse_scan_reset()
  8  call collapse_file() from collapse_single_pmd(), so the file scan
     stops at the decision
  9  give the scan and the collapse a function each: collapse_scan_pmd()
     and collapse_run_pmd()
 10  open-code the entry point that joined them, so each caller owns the
     lock across the boundary and the bool goes
 11  work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA, not once per table
 12  declare the three calls in collapse.h, with the lock rules
 13  MADV_COLLAPSE moves to madvise.c

Behaviour
=========

No functional change is intended.  Nothing here changes which tables get
collapsed, into what, or what MADV_COLLAPSE returns.  The tracepoints are
the one place a change can be seen from outside; the rest is where work
happens, not what it does.

 - Patches 8 and 9: mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd
   fire before the collapse rather than after it.  For an accepted table
   their status field reads SCAN_SUCCEED, where it used to carry what the
   collapse made of the table; that is now for mm_khugepaged_collapse_file
   and mm_collapse_huge_page to report.

Four things move that a reader should not have to find in the diff:

 - Patch 5: khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, so the
   max_ptes_* limits and the defrag setting behind the allocation mask are
   sampled once per pass rather than once per table.  A knob written
   mid-pass takes effect on the next pass instead of the next table.

 - Patch 8: the writeback retry re-runs collapse_file() alone, where it
   used to rescan the page cache first.

 - Patch 9: the file scan runs under mmap_lock, where before the lock was
   given up first.  A file table the scan refuses no longer costs
   khugepaged an unlock, a trip back through khugepaged_do_scan(), a
   relock and a VMA lookup; only a table it goes on to collapse does.

 - Patch 11: which orders a table is scanned for is sampled once per VMA
   rather than once per table.  It cannot widen what a collapse does; the
   order is tested again under the lock the collapse retakes.

For an anonymous table, and for a file table that gets collapsed, the lock
is given up and taken again at exactly the points it was before; the only
difference is that the caller is the one doing it.

DEBUG_VM config, in the five forms run_vmtests.sh runs it.  Every patch
builds, CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE=n included.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

khugepaged.c holds both the users of collapse and the machinery that
performs it.  The daemon's scan loop, the sysfs tunables, MADV_COLLAPSE's
entry point and the collapse itself all sit in one file and reach into
each other freely.  Nothing marks where a user ends and the engine
begins.

Start drawing that line.

Add mm/collapse.h for what the two sides have to agree on:

  - enum scan_result - what the engine hands back;
  - struct collapse_control - the state a request carries.

And two constants move with them:

  - KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT -> COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT;
  - KHUGEPAGED_MIN_MTHP_ORDER -> COLLAPSE_MIN_MTHP_ORDER.

Neither is a fact about the daemon, so both lose the KHUGEPAGED_ prefix.

No functional change.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the interaction between collapse_scan_file() and collapse_file(). They are moving the collapse_file() call up into collapse_single_pmd(), so that the scan stops at the decision, and explaining how this change affects the behavior of writeback retry and mm_khugepaged_collapse_file. The author plans to split the collapse into a scan under mmap_lock and a run without it in future revisions.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about the complexity of collapse_single_pmd() by splitting it into two functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The new functions are designed to work together, with collapse_scan_pmd() scanning one table under mmap_lock and collapse_run_pmd() doing the actual collapse. The author explained that this separation allows for better locking behavior and reduces unnecessary lock drops.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing David Hildenbrand's request to allow both anonymous and file PTEs in the collapse policy. The author explains that khugepaged fills its policy once per scan pass, MADV_COLLAPSE once per call, and introduces a new struct collapse_policy with fields for different types of collapses. The author also removes a NULL check on the collapse_control in collapse_file().
